canonical_statement: The study aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of the 2006 standard and lower-target weight-based heparin protocols and to descriptively compare them with the original 1996 protocol.
The investigation was a retrospective, open-label observational study conducted over 5 months from September 2006 through January 2007.
Protocol selection was left to physician discretion according to the clinical indication rather than randomized assignment.
Patients were excluded if IV heparin was given for less than 24 hours or if the protocol was deliberately modified, except that omission of the bolus was permitted.

population.label: Patients prescribed continuous IV heparin
exclusion_criteria: Deliberate documented protocol changes other than bolus omission

canonical_statement: PTT was monitored for the first 48 hours of continuous IV heparin, or longer when the therapeutic target had not been achieved by 48 hours; an initial PTT was eligible for efficacy analysis only when drawn at least 4 and less than 8 hours after heparin initiation.
Major bleeding and thromboembolic adverse events were assessed over the entire heparin course, whereas protocol compliance was assessed during the first 48 hours.

A convenience sample of 50 patients per 2006 protocol was chosen to match the sample size of the 1996 study; the authors used Mann-Whitney U tests for nonparametric comparisons between the two current protocols with significance set at p<0.05.
The standard protocol was intended for active thromboembolic disease and targeted anti-Xa 0.3-0.7 units/mL, corresponding in the study laboratory to a PTT target of 70-130 seconds.

canonical_statement: Major bleeding was defined as overt bleeding with at least one of: hemoglobin decrease of 20 g/L, transfusion of at least 2 units of blood, or hemorrhage in the retroperitoneum, cranium, or a prosthetic joint.

concept.text: Major bleeding

outcome.definition: Overt bleeding plus hemoglobin decrease >=20 g/L, transfusion >=2 units, or hemorrhage in a specified critical site.

canonical_statement: Of 153 consecutive charts reviewed, 53 patients were excluded, leaving 100 patients: 50 treated with the standard protocol and 50 with the lower-target protocol.
Clinical indications differed substantially by protocol: 68% of standard-protocol patients had DVT or PE, whereas 64% of lower-target-protocol patients had acute coronary syndrome.
The ordered protocol was judged appropriate for 44/50 standard-protocol patients (88%) and 45/50 lower-target-protocol patients (90%).

canonical_statement: The authors concluded that the standard and lower-target protocols appeared similarly effective and safe for rapid therapeutic anticoagulation and appeared to perform at least as well as the original 1996 protocol.
The authors emphasized that protocol violations materially delayed therapeutic anticoagulation and that reinforcement of protocol adherence was important for rapid and safe anticoagulation.
The study was vulnerable to bias from its retrospective observational design, nonprobability sampling, and use of a historical comparator.
The study used a small convenience sample of 50 consecutive patients per protocol over a relatively short period.
Efficacy was analyzed mainly over the first 48 hours, so early target attainment had to be balanced against unmeasured performance in maintaining therapeutic PTT over the full course.
Individual patient data from the 1996 study were irretrievable, so the current protocols could only be compared descriptively, not statistically, with the historical protocol.

Applicability to later practice was limited because the laboratory changed its PTT method in January 2007 and the heparin protocols were modified shortly after the study, including more aggressive reductions for very high PTT values.
